subtype: Approach: pushing through with more effort [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Pallavi,

You asked why I sounded so flat on the phone, so here it is. Since March I have been telling myself I only lack discipline. So I began work at five every morning and stopped taking lunch breaks. I skipped my Saturday football, because rest felt like an excuse. It has gone the other way. Last week I sent a client the wrong file, twice, and my manager said my last report was full of small mistakes I would never have made before. I am more tired than in March, not less. I can see now that more effort was the one thing that could not help. I am going to talk to my doctor this week and tell my manager honestly what is going on. I wanted you to hear it first.

Girish

qa.q: What did Girish give up while trying to be more disciplined?
qa.a: Girish gave up lunch breaks and Saturday football.

qa.q: How does Girish feel about the plan of simply pushing harder?
qa.a: Girish now sees it as a mistake and feels tired and worried.

qa.q: What could work better than pushing through?
qa.a: Girish could rest properly, talk to the doctor, and tell the manager so the workload can be looked at.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt hearing the flat voice, and then the letter?
qa.a: Pallavi may have felt worried about Girish, and glad to be told first.

grounding: Girish believes discipline alone will fix the exhaustion, adds early work and cuts rest, and the errors rise.

passage:
Nitin, you remember when you told me, "Naveen bhai, you look like a ghost"? I laughed and said I just needed discipline. That was my whole theory: I was tired because I was soft.
So I set the alarm for 4.30 and started working two hours before office. I cut Sunday badminton. I stopped taking lunch breaks. For about ten days I felt heroic.
Then the mistakes started. I sent a client the wrong quotation, twice in one week. I forgot our own team review. In the afternoons I'd read the same line five times. My manager asked if something was wrong at home. Nothing was wrong at home. I had taken a tired body and given it less rest.
More effort didn't fix the tiredness, Nitin. It fed it.

qa.q: What time did Naveen set the alarm for?
What does "I felt heroic" reveal about Naveen's feelings at first?
qa.a: Naveen felt proud and determined, believing tiredness was softness that more discipline would cure.

qa.q: What else could Naveen have tried instead of cutting rest?
qa.a: Looking for the causes of the tiredness and talking to the manager about workload, while keeping rest like badminton and lunch breaks.

qa.q: How might the client who got the wrong quotation twice see Naveen's work?
qa.a: The client probably felt frustrated and less confident in Naveen, since the same error happened twice in a week.

grounding: It shows a man who believes he only needs discipline, adding early work and cutting rest, so his errors grow and his exhaustion deepens.

subtype: Approach: pushing through with more effort [Pitfall]
passage:
Shankar has the desk opposite mine in the planning office. In June he started arriving before the cleaners, around 6.30, with a flask and a grim look. He told me, "I've just been lazy. More hours, that's the fix." He stopped coming on the evening chai walk, then stopped eating lunch away from his desk.
I don't know what was going on inside him. I only know what I saw. By July his reports had more mistakes, not fewer. Twice our manager sent them back with red circles. He yawned through the Monday review and snapped at the intern over a spreadsheet. One afternoon I found him staring at his screen with nothing typed. I asked if he wanted to walk. He said, "I can't stop now, I'm already behind."
— Deepika

qa.q: What time did Shankar start arriving in June?
qa.a: Around 6.30, before the cleaners, with a flask.

qa.q: What might Shankar have been feeling when he said "I'm already behind"?
qa.a: He may have felt anxious and trapped, as if stopping would make things worse, though Deepika can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Shankar try instead of adding more hours?
qa.a: He could look at what is causing the exhaustion, talk to the manager, and accept Deepika's offer of a walk as a real break.

qa.q: How does Deepika see Shankar's plan working?
qa.a: Deepika sees it failing: more hours brought more mistakes, red circles from the manager and snapping at the intern.

grounding: It shows a man pushing through with longer hours and less rest, and an onlooker seeing his errors rise and his exhaustion deepen.
